title: AI vs ML vs DL
abstract:
The three words are used interchangeably in casual conversation and they are
not interchangeable at all. This document fixes the relationship precisely:
what each field actually is, the single question that separates ML from
classical programming, the single question that separates DL from ML, why the
distinction has real engineering consequences (data budget, compute budget,
interpretability, debuggability), and how to answer the question in an
interview without hand-waving.

blocks.t: The One-Line Definitions
The three definitions you must be able to recite

items:
Any system that makes a machine mimic human intelligence —
 reasoning, perceiving, planning, deciding. It says nothing about how.

A branch of computer science in which the machine
 learns patterns from data instead of being given explicit rules.

A branch of ML that uses neural networks with many layers so
 that the machine learns the useful features automatically from raw data.

blocks.t:
They are nested, not parallel. Every deep-learning system is a machine-learning
system; every machine-learning system is an AI system. The converse fails in
both directions.

blocks.cap:
AI $\supset$ ML $\supset$ DL. The outer ring contains a great deal of
 classical AI that involves no learning at all: A* search, minimax game trees,
 constraint solvers, and 1980s expert systems.

blocks.t: Why "AI" is the outer ring

Artificial Intelligence as a research programme dates to the 1950s (Turing,
Dartmouth 1956). For its first three decades the dominant approach was
symbolic AI: a human expert writes the knowledge down as rules, and an
inference engine chains those rules together.

Who builds it
Example
rows: Human domain expert dictates facts to a knowledge engineer
"If temperature $>38^\circ$C and cough, then likely influenza"
Doctor types symptoms, gets a diagnosis

blocks.t:
This works beautifully on closed problems — chess has finite legal
moves and a crisp win condition, so Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997 with
essentially search plus hand-tuned evaluation. It fails on fuzzy
problems. Nobody can write down the rule that distinguishes a photograph of a
dog from a photograph of a cat, because that rule does not exist in a form a
human can articulate.
The expert-system wall

Ask yourself: could I write the rule down? If a domain expert can state
the rule in a sentence, symbolic AI works and you probably do not need ML at
all. The moment the expert says "I just know it when I see it", you have hit
the wall that created machine learning.
The Line Between Classical Programming and ML

blocks.cap:
The inputs and outputs are swapped. In classical programming
 you supply the rules and get answers. In machine learning you supply the
 answers and get the rules.

blocks.t: Stated formally
Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the input space and $\mathcal{Y}$ the output space.

Classical programming. A human writes $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$
directly. Given $x$, the machine returns $f(x)$.

Machine learning. A human supplies a dataset
$D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ of examples drawn from an unknown joint
distribution $P(X,Y)$, plus a hypothesis space $\mathcal{H}$ and a loss
$L:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$. The algorithm searches
$\mathcal{H}$ for

where $\Omega$ is a regulariser. The output of the process is the
function itself. This is the entire conceptual content of the phrase "learning
from data".
The canonical worked example
Task: add two numbers.

Classical programming: def add(a, b): return a + b. Three tokens, provably
correct, works for every input forever. Do not use ML here. If you can
write the rule, write the rule.
Task: decide whether an email is spam.
Classical programming attempt:

def is_spam(email):                       # the doomed approach
    if "lottery" in email.body:      return True
    if email.body.count("!") > 3:    return True
    if "free" in email.subject:      return True
    return False

Every rule you add is a rule the spammer reads and routes around: they write
"f r e e", or "1ottery", or move the payload into an image. You are in an
arms race in which you must ship code and they need only change a
character. The rule set becomes unmaintainable and the accuracy still falls.

The ML formulation instead: collect 100{,}000 emails already labelled
spam/not-spam, hand them to a learning algorithm, and let it estimate
$P(\text{spam}\mid \text{words})$. When the spammers change tactics you do not
edit code — you retrain on newer data.
When ML is the right tool
Reach for ML when at least one holds:

items: The rule exists but is too complex to write by hand (spam, credit risk).
The rule exists but nobody can articulate it (is this a dog?).
The rule changes over time and hand-maintenance does not scale (fraud, recommendations).
You want to discover structure a human never looked for (data mining, segmentation).

blocks.t: If none holds, plain code is cheaper, faster, testable and correct.
The Line Between ML and DL

Both learn from data. The difference is who decides what the machine
looks at.

blocks.cap:
The pipeline difference. In ML a human inserts a feature-engineering
 stage. In DL the early layers of the network are the feature-engineering
 stage, and they are learned by the same gradient descent that fits the output.

blocks.t: The sentence to remember

In ML you tell the model what to look at (the features), and it
learns how to decide. In DL you give it raw data, and it learns both
what to look at and how to decide.
Made concrete: "will this candidate be placed?"

ML route. You, the human, decide the model should see CGPA, IQ score,
number of internships, and communication rating. You build those four columns.
The model (say logistic regression) learns four weights. If placement actually
depends on project quality, and you never built that column, the model
can never learn it. Your feature choices are a hard ceiling on accuracy.

DL route. You feed the raw résumé text. Early layers learn character
and word patterns; middle layers learn phrases like "shipped to production";
later layers combine them into an employability signal. No human ever named
those features.
The cost of that convenience

Representation learning is not free. It buys you feature discovery and charges
you in data, compute, and interpretability.

blocks.cap:
The empirical scaling story. Classical ML extracts most of what a
 small dataset contains and then plateaus. Deep networks start worse — they
 have far more parameters and nothing to constrain them — but keep improving
 as data grows.

blocks.t: The single most common junior mistake

Reaching for a neural network on a $5{,}000$-row tabular CSV. On tabular data of
that size, gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost / LightGBM) beat deep networks
almost every time, train in seconds instead of hours, and give you feature
importances you can defend to a stakeholder. Deep learning is the
default for unstructured data (images, audio, text, video), not for
spreadsheets.

blocks.t: Where Related Terms Fit
Vocabulary that gets confused with these three

items:
The umbrella discipline: gathering, cleaning, analysing
 and communicating from data. ML is one tool inside it; a great deal of data
 science is SQL and a chart.

Answering questions a human has already thought to ask
 ("did revenue drop in Q3?"). Descriptive, driven by hypotheses.

Discovering patterns nobody asked about — the
 interesting structure that hides in the data. E.g. after your spam classifier
 is deployed, examining which keywords it learned reveals spammer tactics you
 never knew.

Reporting and dashboards over historical data.
 Backward-looking; ML is forward-looking.

blocks.t: Why ML arrived so late

The core algorithms are old — least squares is from 1805, the perceptron from
1958, backpropagation from the 1970s–80s. Three things were missing and all
three arrived at roughly the same time:

items:
Data. ML runs on data. Before the internet, nobody had it,
 nobody stored it, and storage was expensive.

Hardware. Training needs sustained parallel arithmetic. The GPU,
 built for games, turned out to be exactly the right machine.

Software. Free, high-quality libraries — scikit-learn,
 TensorFlow, PyTorch — collapsed the cost of trying an idea from months to
 minutes.

blocks.t: Code: The Same Problem, Three Ways

# --------------------------------------------------------------------
# TASK: given (CGPA, IQ), predict whether a student is placed.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------

# ---------- 1. SYMBOLIC AI  (rules written by a human) ---------------
def placed_rule_based(cgpa, iq):
    """A human expert dictates the rule. No data involved."""
    if cgpa >= 8.0 and iq >= 100:
        return 1
    if cgpa >= 9.0:                 # brilliant grades excuse a lower IQ
        return 1
    return 0
# Brittle: the thresholds are guesses; nothing adapts when reality shifts.


# ---------- 2. CLASSICAL ML  (rule learned from data) ----------------
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X = np.array([[8.1, 105], [6.2, 88], [9.0, 120], [5.5, 80], [7.4, 99]])
y = np.array([1, 0, 1, 0, 1])

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())
model.fit(X, y)                       # <-- the RULE is learned here
print(model.predict([[7.8, 101]]))    # -> [1]

# The learned rule is inspectable -- this is the interpretability edge:
lr = model.named_steps["logisticregression"]
print("weights:", lr.coef_, "bias:", lr.intercept_)
# NOTE: a HUMAN decided the inputs are CGPA and IQ. That choice caps accuracy.


# ---------- 3. DEEP LEARNING  (features learned too) -----------------
import torch, torch.nn as nn

# Here the input is the RAW RESUME TEXT, not two hand-picked numbers.
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=20000, embedding_dim=64),  # learns word meaning
    nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1),                               # learns what matters
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(),                          # learns combinations
    nn.Linear(32, 1),  nn.Sigmoid(),                       # decides
)
# No human ever wrote "look for the phrase 'shipped to production'".
# The embedding + hidden layers ARE the feature engineering, learned by SGD.
What to notice in the code

In block 2, the line model.fit(X, y) is where a rule is manufactured from
data — that one call is the whole of "machine learning". In block 3, the
Embedding and hidden Linear layers occupy the place where a human
sat in block 2. That substitution is the whole of "deep learning".
Decision Guide
Summary
Everything on one page

items: AI = make machines behave intelligently. Says nothing about method.

ML = a method for AI: learn the rule from data rather than
 being told the rule. Formally, search a hypothesis space for the function
 that minimises empirical risk.

DL = a method for ML: use deep neural networks so the
 features are learned too, not hand-designed.

Classical programming: rules $+$ data $\rightarrow$ answers.
 Machine learning: data $+$ answers $\rightarrow$ rules.
ML: human picks features. DL: network discovers features.

Small/tabular data $\Rightarrow$ classical ML. Large/unstructured data
 $\Rightarrow$ deep learning.

DL's price for automatic features: more data, more compute, less
 interpretability.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Is deep learning better than machine learning?

Wrong framing — DL is ML. On unstructured data with plenty of examples,
deep networks dominate. On tabular data of moderate size, gradient-boosted trees
usually win while being faster and interpretable. Choose by data type and volume.
Q. Give one problem where you would refuse to use ML.

Anything with a known deterministic rule — tax calculation, payroll,
sorting. ML would add error, latency and opacity for no benefit.
Q. Why is deep learning "deep"?

Because of the number of layers. Each successive layer composes the
previous layer's representation into a more abstract one (pixels $\to$ edges
$\to$ textures $\to$ parts $\to$ objects). Depth is what makes automatic feature
learning possible.
Q. Why did DL only take off after 2012?

The algorithms existed for decades. What arrived was the data (internet-scale
labelled sets like ImageNet), the hardware (GPUs), and the software (autodiff
frameworks). AlexNet in 2012 was the moment all three combined.
Q. Where does data mining sit?

Data analysis answers questions you thought to ask; data mining surfaces
patterns you did not know to look for. Both are data science; ML is often the
engine underneath data mining.
